    "# 1. Algorithms for Vortex Panel Methods\n",
    "## 1.1 Aim\n",
    "This assignment aims to implement and study two-dimensional vortex panel methods for predicting the aerodynamic characteristics of a circular cylinder and airfoils.\n",
    "\n",
    "The main objectives: \n",
    "1. To develop algorithms for constant-strength and linear-strength vortex panel methods.\n",
    "2. To implement algorithms in Python using the functions: `vortex_panel_method_0()` and `vortex_panel_method_1()`.\n",
    "3. To verify the implementations using the theoretical pressure distribution around a circular cylinder.\n",
    "4. To investigate the convergence of the solutions by changing the number of panels and the distribution of panel lengths.\n",
    "5. To predict the aerodynamic characteristics and pressure coefficient distributions of one symmetric and one cambered airfoil.\n",
    "6. To investigate how increasing airfoil thickness affects the predictions and identify the limitations of panel methods.\n",
    "\n",
    "The study will help us understand how discretising an airfoil surface affects the numerical solution and how the choice of vortex-strength representation influences the predicted flow field.\n",
    "\n",
    "## 1.2 Introduction to the vortex panel method\n",
    "A panel method is a numerical technique used to estimate the flow around a body by representing its surface as a collection of small straight-line segments called panels. Instead of solving the flow equations at every point in the fluid domain, the method represents the flow using mathematical singularities distributed along the body surface. \\\n",
    "In a vortex panel method, each panel carries a vortex distribution. The strength of this distribution is determined by applying the boundary conditions on the body surface. Once the vortex strengths are known, the velocity and pressure coefficient at different points on the surface can be calculated.\n",
    "\n",
    "For this assignment, two formulations are considered:\n",
    "- **Constant-strength vortex panel method**: The vortex strength remains constant along each panel.\n",
    "- **Linear-strength vortex panel method**: The vortex strength varies linearly along each panel.\n",
    "\n",
    "Both methods are based on the assumptions of steady, two-dimensional, incompressible and inviscid flow. They are useful for studying pressure distributions and lift under attached-flow conditions, but they do not directly model viscous effects such as boundary-layer growth and flow separation.\n",
    "\n",
    "## 1.3 Constant-strength vortex panel method (First-order):\n",
    "In the constant-strength method, the airfoil surface is divided into $N$ straight panels. A single unknown vortex strength, say $\\gamma_j$, is assigned to each panel $j$. \\\n",
    "The vortex strength is then assumed to remain constant over the entire length of the panel. The velocity at any control point is the sum of the freestream velocity and the velocities induced by all vortex panels. \\\n",
    "The no-penetration boundary condition requires that the velocity normal to the surface is zero:  \n",
    "$$ \\mathbf{V}_i \\,.\\, \\mathbf{n}_i = 0$$ \\ \n",
    "where $\\mathbf{V}_i$ is  the total velocity at control point $i$, and $\\mathbf{n}_i$ is the outward unit normal at that point. \n",
    "\n",
    "Applying this condition at all control points produces a system of linear equations. A suitable trailing-edge Kutta condition is also required for an airfoil with a sharp trailing edge. \\\n",
    "The resulting system can be written in the general form as: \n",
    "$$\\mathbf{A \\,\\gamma}=\\mathbf{b}$$ \\\n",
    "where $\\mathbf{A}$ contains the coefficients that represent the vortex influence, $\\mathbf{\\gamma}$ contains the unknown vortex strengths, and $\\mathbf{b}$ represents the contribution of the freestream velocity and the imposed boundary conditions.\n",
    "\n",
    "**Algorithm:** \n",
    "1. Generation of coordinates describing the body surface.\n",
    "2. Divide the surface into $N$ straight panels.\n",
    "3. Calculate the length, the midpoint, tangent and outward normal of each panel.\n",
    "4. Calculate the velocity induced by each unit-strength vortex panel at every control point.\n",
    "5. Assemble the influence coefficient matrix.\n",
    "6. Apply the no-penetration boundary condition and the appropriate Kutta condition.\n",
    "7. Solve the resulting linear system for the vortex strengths.\n",
    "8. Calculate the tangential velocity at each control point.\n",
    "9. Calculate the pressure coefficient at each control point.\n",
    "10. Return the calculated aerodynamic quantities and repeat the procedure for other discretisations during the convergence study.\n",
    "\n",
    "## 1.4 Linear-strength vortex panel method (Second-order):\n",
    "In the linear-strength method, the vortex strength varies linearly along each panel rather than remaining constant. The variation over panel $j$ can be given as: \n",
    "$$\\gamma_j(s) = \\gamma_{j,1}+\\frac{s}{L_j}(\\gamma_{j,2}-\\gamma_{j,1})$$\n",
    "where:\n",
    "- $s$ is the distance measured from the beginning of the panel,\n",
    "- $L_j$ is the panel length,\n",
    "- $\\gamma_{j,1}$ and $\\gamma_{j,2}$ are the vortex strengths at the two end points.\n",
    "\n",
    "This representation allows the vortex distribution to change along the body surface. It can represent variations in circulation more smoothly than a piecewise-constant distribution, although its accuracy still depends on the formulation, boundary conditions and panel distribution.\n",
    "\n",
    "The end point strengths of neighbouring panels must be handled consistently. The system must also include the required boundary conditions and a suitable Kutta condition.\n",
    "\n",
    "**Algorithm:**\n",
    "1. Generate the body coordinates and divide the surface into $N$ panels.\n",
    "2. Calculate the panel lengths, midpoints, tangents and normals.\n",
    "3. Represent the vortex strength on each panel using a linear variation between its endpoint values.\n",
    "4. Calculate the velocity induced by the linearly varying vortex distribution at each control point.\n",
    "5. Assemble the influence coefficient matrix for the unknown endpoint strengths.\n",
    "6. Apply the no-penetration boundary condition at all control points.\n",
    "7. Apply the appropriate trailing edge Kutta condition.\n",
    "8. Solve the resulting system for the vortex strengths.\n",
    "9. Calculate the tangential velocity and pressure coefficient along the surface.\n",
    "10. Repeat the calculation with different panel counts and panel distributions to study convergence.\n",
    "\n",
    "The linear-strength formulation is implemented using the integral expressions for the linearly varying vortex strength, following the formulation described in _Han Liu (2018)_. It is not sufficient to obtain this method by simply interpolating the results of the constant-strength method."
   ]
  },

    "## 2. Python Implementation\n",
    "\n",
    "### 2.1 Implementation of `vortex_panel_method_0()`\n",
    "This is the first Python function that implements the constant-strength vortex panel method. It converts the mathematical formulation into a numerical procedure that can be used for different body geometries and flow conditions. \\\n",
    "The function accepts the airfoil coordinates, freestream conditions and numerical settings as input. It returns the calculated vortex strengths, surface velocities, pressure coefficients and relevant aerodynamic coefficients.\n",
    "\n",
    "The implementation involves the following operations:\n",
    "1. Read the body coordinates and construct the panels.\n",
    "2. Calculate the geometric properties of each panel\n",
    "3. Construct the influence coefficient matrix\n",
    "4. Apply the surface boundary conditions and Kutta condition.\n",
    "5. Solve the linear system.\n",
    "6. Calculate the surface velocity and pressure coefficient.\n",
    "7. Return the results in a structured form.\n",
    "\n",
    "### 2.2 Implementation of `vortex_panel_method_1()`\n",
    "The second function implements the linear-strength vortex panel method. It follows a similar overall procedure, but the unknowns and influence coefficients are formulated using the linearly varying vortex strength. \\\n",
    "The main difference lies in the calculation of the induced velocity and the construction of the system of equations. Since the vortex strength varies along each panel, the corresponding influence integrals must account for this variation. \\\n",
    "The function returns the same type of aerodynamic quantities as the constant-strength method wherever possible. This makes it easier to compare the two methods under identical conditions.\n",
    "\n",
    "### 2.3 Input arguments, outputs and numerical procedure\n",
    "The following table describes a suitable interface for both functions.\n",
    "|Input or Output|Description|\n",
    "|-----|------|\n",
    "|`x`,`y`|Coordinates defining the body surface|\n",
    "|`U_inf`|Freestream velocity magnitude|\n",
    "|`alpha`|Angle of attack|\n",
    "|`panel_distribution`|Choice of uniform or cosine-spaced discretisation|\n",
    "|`gamma`|Calculated vortex strength distribution|\n",
    "|`V_t`|Tangential velocity at the control points|\n",
    "|`Cp`|Surface pressure coefficient|\n",
    "|`Cl`|Lift coefficient|\n",
    "\n",
    "The pressure coefficient is calculated from the local tangential velocity using Bernoulli's equation: \\\n",
    "$$C_p = \\frac{p - p_{\\infty}}{\\frac{1}{2} \\rho U^2_{\\infty}} = 1- (\\frac{V_t}{U_{\\infty}})^2$$\n",
    "here $p_{\\infty}$ and $U_{\\infty}$ are the freestream static pressure and velocity, respectively."
   ]

    "#importing libraries\n",
    "import numpy as np\n",
    "import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n",
    "\n",
    "from numpy import pi, sin, cos, sqrt\n",
    "from numpy.linalg import solve\n",
    "\n",
    "plt.rcParams['figure.figsize']=(8,5)\n",
    "plt.rcParams['font.family']='Times New Roman'\n",
    "plt.rcParams['font.size'] = 12\n",
    "plt.rcParams['axes.grid'] = True"

   "source": [
    "def naca_airfoil(m,p,t,N=100, spacing= 'cosine'):\n",
    "    if spacing == 'cosine':\n",
    "        beta = np.linspace(0,pi,N)\n",
    "        x=0.5*(1-np.cos(beta))\n",
    "    else:\n",
    "        x=np.linspace(0,1,N)\n",
    "\n",
    "    yt = 5*t*(0.2969*np.sqrt(x)-0.1260*x - 0.35168*x**2 + 0.2843*x**3 - 0.1015*x**4)\n",
    "    yc= np.zeros_like(x)\n",
    "    dyc_dx = np.zeros_like(x)\n",
    "\n",
    "    for i in range(N):\n",
    "        if x[i]<p and p != 0:\n",
    "            yc[i] = (m/p**2)*(2*p*x[i] - x[i]**2)\n",
    "            dyc_dx[i]=(2*m/p**2)*(p-x[i])\n",
    "        elif p!=0:\n",
    "            yc[i]=(m/(1-p)**2)*((1-2*p)+2*p*x[i]-x[i]**2)\n",
    "            dyc_dx[i]=(2*m/(1-p)**2)*(p-x[i])\n",
    "    theta = np.arctan(dyc_dx)\n",
    "\n",
    "    xu = x-yt*np.sin(theta)\n",
    "    yu = yc+yt*np.cos(theta)\n",
    "\n",
    "    xl=x+yt*np.sin(theta)\n",
    "    yl=yc-yt*np.cos(theta)\n",
    "\n",
    "    X=np.concatenate((xu[::-1], xl[1:]))\n",
    "    Y=np.concatenate((yu[::-1], yl[1:]))\n",
    "\n",
    "    return X,Y"
   ]
  },

   "source": [
    "#generating panel\n",
    "def panel_geometry(x,y):\n",
    "    x1 = x[:-1]\n",
    "    y1 = y[:-1]\n",
    "    x2=x[1:]\n",
    "    y2=y[1:]\n",
    "\n",
    "    dx = x2-x1\n",
    "    dy = y2-y1\n",
    "\n",
    "    length=np.sqrt(dx**2 + dy**2)\n",
    "\n",
    "    xc= 0.5*(x1+x2)\n",
    "    yc = 0.5*(y1+y2)\n",
    "\n",
    "    theta = np.arctan2(dy,dx)\n",
    "\n",
    "    return{'x1': x1,\n",
    "        'y1': y1,\n",
    "        'x2': x2,\n",
    "        'y2': y2,\n",
    "        'xc': xc,\n",
    "        'yc': yc,\n",
    "        'length': length,\n",
    "        'theta': theta}"
   ]

    "## 3. Verification using a circular cylinder\n",
    "### 3.1 Geometry and analytical solution\n",
    "For a cylinder of radius R in a uniform freestream, with no circulation, the tangential velocity at the surface is:\n",
    "$$V_{\\theta} = -2U_{\\infty} \\sin \\theta$$\n",
    "and the corresponding pressure coefficient is given by:\n",
    "$$C_p = 1-4 \\sin^2 \\theta$$\n",
    "where $\\theta$ is measured around the cylinder from the forward stagnation point.\n",
    "\n",
    "The cylinder is discretised using straight panels. Both vortex panel methods are then applied using the same geometry and freestream conditions.\n",
    "\n",
    "### 3.2 Results for different number of panels\n",
    "The number of panels is varied to investigate the effect of discretisation. Suitable initial cases are $N=20, 40, 80$ and $160$, provided the implementations remain numerically stable.\n",
    "For each case, the calculated pressure coefficient is plotted against the angular position and compared with the analytical solution.\n",
    "\n",
    "The errors can be calculated as:\n",
    "$$E_{max} = \\max_{i} |C_{p,i} - C^{\\text{exact}}_{p,i}|$$\n",
    "$$E_{RMS} = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{N} \\sum{i=1}^{N} (C_{p,i} - C_{p,i}^{\\text{exact}})^2}$$\n",
    "\n",
    "The analytical values are evaluated at the same angular positions as the numerical control points.\n",
    "\n",
    "### 3.3 Convergence study\n",
    "The convergence study examines whether the numerical solution approaches the analytical solution as the panel count increases. \\\n",
    "The expected trend is that a consistent and correctly implemented method increasingly resolves the smooth circular geometry and its pressure distribution as the panels become smaller. \\\n",
    "A failure to converge, or an error that remains large as the panel count increases, may indicate an implementation or formulation problem rather than an inherent limitation of the panel method.\n"
   ]
  },

    "#defining the cylinder\n",
    "\n",
    "def cylinder_geometry(N, R=1.0):\n",
    "    theta = np.linspace(0,2*pi, N+1)\n",
    "    x=R*np.cos(theta)\n",
    "    y=R*np.sin(theta)\n",
    "\n",
    "    return x,y"

    "#finding Cp for cylinder\n",
    "\n",
    "def cylinder_analytical_cp(theta):\n",
    "    return 1-4*np.sin(theta)**2\n",

    "#Numerical Cp for cylinder\n",
    "def cylinder_panel_solver(N, R=1.0,U_inf=1.0):\n",
    "    x,y = cylinder_geometry(N,R)\n",
    "\n",
    "    x1,y1 = x[:-1], y[:-1]\n",
    "    x2,y2 = x[1:], y[1:]\n",
    "\n",
    "    dx = x2-x1\n",
    "    dy = y2-y1\n",
    "    length = np.sqrt(dx**2+dy**2)\n",
    "\n",
    "    tx=dx/length\n",
    "    ty = dy/length\n",
    "\n",
    "    nx= ty\n",
    "    ny= -tx\n",
    "\n",
    "    xc = 0.5*(x1+x2)\n",
    "    yc=0.5*(y1+y2)\n",
    "\n",
    "    q,w = np.polynomial.legendre.leggauss(80)\n",
    "\n",
    "    A= np.zeros((N, N))\n",
    "    T=np.zeros((N,N))\n",
    "\n",
    "    for i in range(N):\n",
    "        for j in range(N):\n",
    "            if j==i:\n",
    "                A[i,j] = 0.5\n",
    "                T[i,j]=0.0\n",
    "                continue\n",
    "            s=0.5*(q+1)\n",
    "\n",
    "            xp=x1[j]+s*dx[j]\n",
    "            yp=y1[j]+s*dy[j]\n",
    "\n",
    "            rx=xc[i]-xp\n",
    "            ry=yc[i]-yp\n",
    "\n",
    "            r2=rx**2+ry**2\n",
    "\n",
    "            #induced velocity due to unit source panel\n",
    "            u = np.sum(w*rx/r2)*length[j]/(4*pi)\n",
    "            v=np.sum(w*ry/r2)*length[j]/(4*pi)\n",
    "\n",
    "            A[i,j]=u*nx[i]+v*ny[i]\n",
    "            T[i,j]=u*tx[i]+v*ty[i]\n",
    "\n",
    "    b=-U_inf*nx\n",
    "    sigma = np.linalg.solve(A,b)\n",
    "    Vt = U_inf*tx+ T @ sigma\n",
    "    Cp = 1-(Vt/U_inf)**2\n",
    "\n",
    "    theta = np.arctan2(yc,xc)\n",
    "    return theta, Vt, Cp, sigma"
   ]
  },

    "def calculate_errors(Cp_numerical, Cp_exact):\n",
    "\n",
    "    error = Cp_numerical - Cp_exact\n",
    "\n",
    "    max_error = np.max(np.abs(error))\n",
    "\n",
    "    rms_error = np.sqrt(np.mean(error**2))\n",
    "\n",
    "    return max_error, rms_error\n",
    "\n",
    "\n",
    "max_error, rms_error = calculate_errors(\n",
    "    Cp_numerical, Cp_exact\n",
    ")\n",
    "\n",
    "print(\"Maximum absolute error =\", max_error)\n",
    "print(\"Root Mean Square Error =\", rms_error)\n",
    "\n",
    "panel_counts = [10, 20, 40, 80, 160]\n",
    "\n",
    "max_errors = []\n",
    "rms_errors = []\n",
    "\n",
    "for N in panel_counts:\n",
    "\n",
    "    # Numerical panel solution\n",
    "    theta, Vt, Cp_numerical, sigma = cylinder_panel_solver(\n",
    "        N=N,\n",
    "        R=1.0,\n",
    "        U_inf=1.0\n",
    "    )\n",
    "\n",
    "    # Analytical solution at the same control points\n",
    "    Cp_exact = cylinder_analytical_cp(theta)\n",
    "\n",
    "    # Calculate errors\n",
    "    max_error, rms_error = calculate_errors(\n",
    "        Cp_numerical, Cp_exact\n",
    "    )\n",
    "\n",
    "    max_errors.append(max_error)\n",
    "    rms_errors.append(rms_error)\n",
    "\n",
    "\n",
    "print(\"Number of panels | Maximum error | RMS error\")\n",
    "\n",
    "for i in range(len(panel_counts)):\n",
    "    print(\n",
    "        f\"{panel_counts[i]:16d} | \"\n",
    "        f\"{max_errors[i]:13.6e} | \"\n",
    "        f\"{rms_errors[i]:10.6e}\"\n",
    "    )\n",
    "\n",
    "plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))\n",
    "\n",
    "plt.loglog(panel_counts, max_errors, 'ro-',\n",
    "           label='Maximum error')\n",
    "\n",
    "plt.loglog(panel_counts, rms_errors, 'bs-',\n",
    "           label='RMS error')\n",
    "\n",
    "plt.xlabel('Number of panels')\n",
    "plt.ylabel('Error')\n",
    "plt.title('Convergence Study for Circular Cylinder')\n",
    "\n",
    "plt.legend()\n",

   "source": [
    "## 4. Verification using symmetric and non-symmetric airfoils\n",
    "### 4.1 Airfoil geometry and computational setup\n",
    "The two airfoils selected for this study are:\n",
    "- **NACA 0012:** A symmetric airfoil with $12\\%$ thickness-to-chord ratio and zero camber.\n",
    "- **NACA 4412:** A cambered airfoil with $12\\%$ thickness-to-chord ratio, maximum camber of $4\\%$ of the chord, and maximum camber location at $40\\%$ of the chord.\n",
    "\n",
    "The airfoil coordinates are generated using the standard NACA four-digit geometry equations. The coordinates are then discretised into straight panels. The same freestream conditions are used for both vortex panel methods to ensure a fair comparison. \\\n",
    "For airfoils with a sharp trailing edge, the geometry and panel orientation must be chosen consistently with the Kutta condition.\n",
    "\n",
    "### 4.2 Effect of number of panels\n",
    "The panel count is varied while keeping the airfoil geometry, angle of attack, and panel-spacing strategy fixed.\n",
    "\n",
    "For each discretisation, the pressure coefficient distribution is calculated using the above-mentioned methods. The results are compared to determine whether increasing the number of panels changes the predicted pressure distribution and aerodynamic coefficients. \\\n",
    "\n",
    "The study investigates:\n",
    "1. The pressure distribution becomes stable as the panel count increases.\n",
    "2. The predicted lift coefficient changes significantly with panel count.\n",
    "3. The constant and linear methods converge at similar rates.\n",
    "4. The pressure distribution near the leading edge is sensitive to discretisation.\n",
    "\n",
    "### 4.3 Effects of panel-length distribution\n",
    "Two panel distributions are considered: uniform spacing and cosine spacing.\n",
    "In uniform spacing, the panels have approximately equal lengths along the airfoil surface. This is straightforward to implement, but it may not provide enough resolution in regions where the surface curvature and pressure gradients change rapidly.\\\n",
    "Cosine spacing clusters the points near the leading and trailing edges. A common chordwise distribution is:\n",
    "$$x_i = \\frac{c}{2}[1-cos(\\frac{i\\pi}{N})], \\,{i=0,...,N}$$\n",
    "\n",
    "where $c$ is the chord length.\n",
    "This distribution provides more points near the leading and trailing edges and fewer near the middle of the chord. For a closed airfoil, the upper and lower surface coordinates must be generated and ordered consistently.\n",
    "\n",
    "### 4.4 Comparison of constant and linear strength methods\n",
    "The two methods are compared using the same airfoil geometry, freestream conditions and panel distributions.\n",
    "\n",
    "The constant-strength method represents the vortex strength as piecewise constant, whereas the linear-strength method permits a linear variation along the surface panels. The latter offers a more flexible representation of the vortex distribution, but it also requires a more involved influence-coefficient formulation.\n",
    "\n",
    "A more flexible representation does not automatically guarantee greater accuracy. The relative performance is assessed using convergence results and an appropriate reference solution."
   ]
  },
